title: No condemnation (Romans 8:1–17)
hook: there is now no condemnation; we cry Abba, Father
carry: a child at home, not a prisoner on trial

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was talaiporos, wretched: the good I want, I don't do. Your line was who shall deliver me?

Some people carry a courtroom around inside their heads, with a prosecutor who never takes a day off. You forgot the birthday: guilty. You snapped at the kids: guilty. That thing from ninth grade: still guilty, somehow, at three in the morning. The case is never closed. Paul ended chapter seven crying out, who shall deliver me? Now he turns the page, and chapter eight, which many readers call the high point of the whole letter, opens with a verdict. And it's very bad news for the prosecutor.
screen: `A COURTROOM INSIDE YOUR HEAD.` → `THE CASE IS NEVER CLOSED.` → `CHAPTER EIGHT OPENS WITH A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: The verdict, in the King James Bible: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." The Greek word is katakrima, and it's more than a guilty verdict; it's the sentence that follows, the penalty handed down. Not less. None. And not someday: now, an echo of the hinge a few days ago, but now. Then he explains how: the Spirit. In chapter seven the Spirit was hardly mentioned; in chapter eight the Spirit is everywhere, living in people, giving life, leading them. And the courtroom turns into a family room: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Abba is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke at home, the word a child uses for a father, close and warm. Mark's Gospel says Jesus himself prayed Abba in the garden the night before he died. Paul keeps it in Aramaic even writing in Greek to Rome, as if some words shouldn't be translated. Adoption was serious in Roman law: an adopted son became a full heir, with a new name and a new standing. And the Spirit itself, Paul says, bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. So the prosecutor doesn't get the last word. A father does. Christians of every church say that doesn't make wrong things right; it means a person isn't defined by them. You can still say sorry, and change. But you do it as a child at home, not as a prisoner on trial.
screen: `KATAKRIMA: THE SENTENCE HANDED DOWN.` · `NOW: NOT SOMEDAY.` · `THE SPIRIT OF ADOPTION.` · `ABBA: A CHILD'S WORD FOR FATHER.` · then, large: `THERE IS THEREFORE NOW NO CONDEMNATION.`

segments.voice: Listen for the prosecutor in your head and find one charge it keeps bringing up, something old you've already apologized for or can't fix now; hear it clearly, once, then imagine the case closed, the file set down, a little further away with each breath out. If it comes back, that's all right; set it down again. If you pray, say the old family word, Abba, and rest there.
No condemnation. Katakrima in Greek: the sentence, the penalty. Paul says for those in Christ there is none, and there is none now.
Your line: a child at home, not a prisoner on trial. That's day three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Romans 8:1, and many use the word Abba in personal prayer, the way Jesus did in the garden; Romans 8 is often read at baptisms and funerals.

chat.meaning: Paul says there is now no condemnation in Christ. That doesn't make wrong things right; it means a person isn't defined by them.

notes: Katakrima as the penalty/sentence rather than only the verdict: standard in lexicons; confirm.
'In chapter seven the Spirit was hardly mentioned': the Spirit appears in 7:6 and 7:14 ('the law is spiritual'); 'hardly' is deliberate. Confirm.
Abba as 'a child's word' for father: the older claim that it means 'daddy' is contested (e.g. James Barr, 1988); the script avoids 'daddy' and says 'close and warm'. Confirm.
Roman adoption (full heir, new name, new standing): simplified; confirm.
The 'Christians of every church say' sentence summarizes a broad consensus; confirm.
